Frozen in a Frame: The Velocity Blind Spot in JEPA World Models

Tinghe Zhang Affiliation: Tsinghua University Affiliation: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences Affiliation: Northeastern University    Chunyu Liu Affiliation: Tsinghua University    Yu Leon Liu Affiliation: Tsinghua University Affiliation: Harvard University    Zerui Zhao Affiliation: Tsinghua University Affiliation: University of Oxford    Jiaheng Chen Affiliation: Northeastern University    Yucheng Xiao Affiliation: Northeastern University    Jiaxing Li Affiliation: Northeastern University    Yunlong Wang Affiliation: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences    Alex Lamb Affiliation: Tsinghua University
Abstract

Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) for world modeling train an encoder so a predictor maps a current embedding and action to the next frame’s embedding, always from a single rendered frame. This has a structural blind spot: a renderer without motion blur draws a scene from configuration alone, so a single-frame embedding carries no velocity information, for any encoder, including the official released LeWM weights. We confirm this on official checkpoints across four real benchmarks (PushT, Reacher, Cube, TwoRoom): every linear velocity probe sits at or below chance while position probes reach R2≈0.95R^{2}\approx 0.95. We introduce RateIdent, a three-stage diagnostic protocol, and TI-JEPA, a lightweight fix splitting the latent into a pose code and an explicit finite-difference motion code, predicted jointly. Across three physically grounded environments, TI-JEPA gives a significant, seed-robust gain on a stop-at-goal planning task over a matched-memory baseline, e.g. 55% lower final distance on Pendulum (p=3.2×10−10p=3.2\times 10^{-10}) and 64% on CartPole (p=5.1×10−15p=5.1\times 10^{-15}). We reproduce this at official ViT-Tiny plus AdaLN-transformer scale, then push the same recipe onto real dm_control Reacher photographs trained from scratch, where TI-JEPA’s branch separation exceeds the memory-having baseline’s by roughly 38×38\times, the paper’s largest margin. Against a same-footprint recurrent RSSM-style predictor, TI-JEPA matches or beats its rollout accuracy on two of three environments, stays separately probeable for pose and motion, and wins outright on the most coupled one. A checkable formal argument and six evaluated environments show single-frame targets are the wrong object to predict when velocity matters, and a small, interpretable structural change fixes it with no privileged supervision. Code, checkpoints, and the project page are linked below the title.

1 Introduction

A next-frame joint-embedding predictive architecture, or JEPA, learns to predict the embedding of the next observation from the embedding of the current one and the action taken. When this prediction gets accurate, it is tempting to say the model understands the dynamics of the scene. We point to a important gap between training signal and that claim. The prediction target, zt+1=E⁡(ot+1)z_{t+1}=E(o_{t+1}), is an embedding of one rendered frame. A single still frame cannot carry the instantaneous rate of change of the scene’s configuration: nothing in one frame’s pixels encodes it, no motion blur, no stroboscopic exposure, no on-screen speed readout. This is a property of how the target is built, not of any particular encoder’s capacity or training recipe. A bigger network trained longer does not fix it. The argument holds for the population-optimal predictor under any measurable encoder.

Figure 1 previews the full evidence chain in one image. Three panels cover the three diagnostics we use throughout the paper: a linear probe ladder, a kill experiment built from two physically identical-looking frames with opposite velocity, and a downstream planning task. Nine environment and scale combinations, spanning official checkpoints, our own small models, and official-scale reruns, show the same pattern every time. Figure 3 makes the underlying construction concrete on real rendered frames from all four environments we build or train on: two rollouts sharing the same starting configuration but opposite velocity are pixel-identical at t=0t{=}0 and visibly diverge afterward under the real physics.

Contributions. We organize the paper around three contributions.

First, a formal proposition, checkable in a few minutes, that characterizes exactly which physical quantities a single-frame JEPA target can and cannot identify (Section 4), with two corollaries: the L2L^{2}-optimal predictor cannot use velocity even though its raw target technically depends on it, and a single static goal image cannot specify a target velocity for goal-conditioned planning. We confirm this empirically on the officially released LeWM checkpoints across four real benchmarks with zero retraining: every single-frame, pair, and three-frame-window linear velocity probe sits at or below its own shuffled-label chance floor, while position decoding on the same embeddings reaches R2≈0.94R^{2}\approx 0.94–0.980.98.

Second, RateIdent and TI-JEPA. RateIdent is an environment-agnostic three-rung protocol, probe ladder, kill experiment, and inertial planning, implemented once and reused unmodified across six environments with different action spaces, dimensionalities, and renderers. TI-JEPA is a lightweight fix with no privileged supervision: split the latent into a single-frame pose code and an explicit finite-difference motion code, and predict both jointly. Across three physically grounded environments, InertiaBall, Pendulum, and CartPole, TI-JEPA gives statistically significant, seed-robust gains on a stop-at-goal control task over a matched-memory baseline. We reproduce the theory’s central guarantee, exact-zero branch separation for the memoryless baseline, at official ViT-Tiny plus AdaLN-transformer scale on two environments, and we push the identical recipe onto real dm_control Reacher photographs (Tassa et al., 2018) trained from scratch, where TI-JEPA’s kill-experiment margin over the memory-having baseline is the largest in the paper.

Third, a same-footprint comparison against the most natural competing fix: a recurrent, RSSM-style predictor aggregator in the spirit of PlaNet and Dreamer. The probe-ladder result does not change, because it depends only on the training target, not on how the predictor aggregates history, so the recurrent aggregator’s single-frame code stays at chance like every other arm. The real value of the comparison is diagnostic. A recurrent hidden state folds pose and motion into one opaque vector; it ties or beats TI-JEPA’s raw rollout accuracy on two of three environments, but it cannot be queried for either quantity on its own. TI-JEPA’s explicit split stays linearly readable and wins outright on the environment with the most coupled dynamics.

2 Related Work

Joint-embedding world models. Joint-embedding predictive architectures learn by predicting missing input in embedding space rather than pixel space (LeCun & Courant, 2022); I-JEPA showed this for static images (Assran et al., 2023), and V-JEPA extended it to masked spatio-temporal video patches (Bardes et al., 2024; Assran et al., 2025). The collapse-preventing regularizers behind this line, variance/covariance penalties (Bardes et al., 2022), stop-gradient asymmetry (Grill et al., 2022; Chen & He, 2021), and self-distillation (Caron et al., 2021), are direct ancestors of the SIGReg term LeWM uses. LeWM (Maes et al., 2026) applies this recipe to world modeling with a single next-frame embedding as the target; 2026 follow-ups keep that same single-frame target while changing other parts of the recipe, grounding a pair of embeddings in proprioception (Yan et al., 2026), inverting the embedding difference into the causing action (Zhang et al., 2026b), moving the regularizer to random subspaces (Zhao et al., 2026), or speeding up multi-step prediction (Gao & Xu, 2026) — none changes what the target is a function of. Sobal et al. observed the resulting drift toward slow, static features (Sobal et al., 2022), the empirical ancestor of the phenomenon we formalize; Klindt et al. showed a single frame does linearly identify a Gaussian latent up to rotation (Klindt et al., 2026), assuming the quantity of interest is already present in that frame, exactly the case our proposition shows fails for a generic second-order physical system. Zhang et al. analyze the identifiability and latent geometry of this same class of joint-embedding world models (Zhang et al., 2026a). Position probes stay high whether or not velocity is identifiable, so strong probe numbers alone are not evidence either way.

Recurrent belief-state world models. A separate, older line of work never commits to a single-frame embedding as the state at all. World Models trains a recurrent hidden state on top of a frame encoder (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018); PlaNet’s recurrent state-space model formalizes this as a belief state mixing a deterministic recurrent path with a stochastic component across a trajectory (Hafner et al., 2018), and Dreamer and its successors train a policy directly on imagined rollouts through that belief state (Hafner et al., 2020a; Hafner et al., 2023); the same line frames action and perception as divergence minimization (Hafner et al., 2020b). Earlier model-based control work makes the analogous point for video-prediction, locally linear, or ensemble dynamics models (Kaiser et al., 2019; Watter et al., 2015; Finn & Levine, 2017; Nagabandi et al., 2018; Chua et al., 2018). Because a recurrent belief state need not be a deterministic function of the current frame alone, our single-frame hypothesis does not apply to it, leaving a narrower, testable question: does a same-footprint recurrent aggregator, bolted onto our exact single-frame-target pipeline, close the gap without the larger architectural change of a full belief state? Section 7.5 answers this directly, with results that favor each side on different environments.

Disentangling content from motion. A third line separates static content from time-varying motion directly in pixel space: DrNet uses adversarial pressure to push a stationary content code and a time-varying pose code apart (Denton & Birodkar, 2017), MCnet uses two asymmetric pathways for the same purpose (Villegas et al., 2017), and MoCoGAN and later disentangled sequential models extend the idea to generative video and motion transfer (Tulyakov et al., 2018; Hsieh et al., 2018; Li & Mandt, 2018); structured, physically informed latents have also been used directly for video prediction and planning (Jaques et al., 2020; Kossen et al., 2020; Franceschi et al., 2020; Seo et al., 2023). TI-JEPA’s pose/motion split is the same idea, roughly a decade later, applied to embedding-space prediction for control rather than pixel-space generation, with a different mechanism: a bias-free finite difference gives a checkable guarantee, identical repeated frames give exactly zero decoded velocity, rather than an adversarial or architectural pressure that only encourages the split. This connects to a broader literature on nonlinear identifiability and causal representation learning (Hyvärinen & Morioka, 2017; Khemakhem et al., 2022; Locatello et al., 2019; Schölkopf et al., 2021); we target a specific, previously informal claim about kinematic state rather than a general identifiability result.

3 Preliminaries

We follow LeWM’s own formulation. An encoder EE maps an observation oto_{t} to zt=E⁡(ot)z_{t}=E(o_{t}); an action encoder maps ata_{t} to an action embedding; a predictor, an autoregressive transformer with AdaLN-zero conditioning on the action embedding, maps a window of embeddings and actions to a predicted z^t+1\hat{z}_{t+1}. Training minimizes Lpred=‖z^t+1−zt+1‖2L_{\mathrm{pred}}=\|\hat{z}_{t+1}-z_{t+1}\|^{2} plus a SIGReg isotropic-Gaussian regularizer on the marginal distribution of zz, with no negative pairs and no stop-gradient target. Two details of the official recipe matter for everything that follows. The predictor’s input is allowed a short history window, three frames in the official configuration, but the target it is trained to match is always a single frame’s embedding. And the released PushT environment sets its damping parameter to zero, which in the underlying physics engine’s convention is maximal per-step damping rather than frictionless motion, a property of the official benchmark we verified directly, and part of why the official benchmarks alone cannot exercise the gap we study.

4 Target Identifiability

Setup. A rendering map g:𝒬→𝒪g:\mathcal{Q}\to\mathcal{O} produces ot=g⁡(qt)o_{t}=g(q_{t}) from the instantaneous configuration qtq_{t} alone. We call this assumption (P), instantaneous rendering, and it is true of every renderer without motion blur. A single-frame encoder E:𝒪→𝒵E:\mathcal{O}\to\mathcal{Z} produces zt=E⁡(ot)z_{t}=E(o_{t}). We call this assumption (A), and it is true of every next-frame JEPA world model we are aware of.

Proposition 1. Under (P) and (A), zt=h⁡(qt)z_{t}=h(q_{t}) almost surely, for h:=E∘gh:=E\circ g. Hence: (1) σ⁡(zt)⊆σ⁡(qt)\sigma(z_{t})\subseteq\sigma(q_{t}), so anything identifiable from ztz_{t} is identifiable from qtq_{t} alone; (2) if q˙t\dot{q}_{t} is not almost surely a measurable function of qtq_{t} alone, which is the generic case for any system whose initial velocity is not itself determined by position, then q˙t\dot{q}_{t} is not identifiable from ztz_{t}, for any encoder EE, however expressive; (3) zt⟂q˙t|qtz_{t}\perp\dot{q}_{t}\mid q_{t}.

The proof is a two-line data-processing argument, given in full in Appendix A. Its value is pointing this argument at the specific target construction every next-frame JEPA makes, turning an intuition, single frames cannot show speed, into a falsifiable, checkable claim about a specific loss function.

Corollary 1. The population-risk minimizer of the JEPA prediction loss satisfies pred⋆(z,a)=𝔼[zt+1∣zt=z,at=a]\mathrm{pred}^{\star}(z,a)=\mathbb{E}[z_{t+1}\mid z_{t}=z,a_{t}=a], the transition averaged over q˙t\dot{q}_{t}. For any genuinely second-order system, this differs from the true, velocity-conditioned transition with positive probability. Two states with identical qtq_{t} but opposite q˙t\dot{q}_{t} have identical ztz_{t} and hence identical pred⋆\mathrm{pred}^{\star}: the model’s best possible rollout cannot tell them apart. This is the formal statement behind the kill experiment in Section 6.

Corollary 2. A goal-conditioned planning cost J=‖zH−E⁡(og)‖2J=\|z_{H}-E(o_{g})\|^{2} built from a single static goal frame is constant along the set of states sharing the goal configuration: it cannot express a preference between arriving and stopping versus arriving fast and coasting through. This is the formal reason the stop-at-goal task in Protocol C is diagnostic.

Three constructions restore identifiability, formalized in Appendix A: encoding a multi-frame window rather than a single frame, which is what the official predictor’s input window already does but does not by itself change the target; a structured target z=(q,v)z=(q,v) with vv an explicit finite-difference function of a window, predicted jointly, which is TI-JEPA; and predicting the transition Δ​zt\Delta z_{t} directly rather than zt+1z_{t+1}. We implement the first two together. The proof only uses Borel measurability, so it holds for any encoder family, from a small CNN (LeCun et al., 2015) to an ImageNet-scale ViT (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020), and it covers pair-based fixes like PSG-JEPA and Delta-JEPA as a special case of the first construction.

5 Method: TI-JEPA

Figure 2 contrasts the two computational graphs. TI-JEPA’s encoder produces a pose code qt=Eq​(ot)q_{t}=E_{q}(o_{t}) from a single frame and a motion code vt=MLPbias​-​free(finite differences of qt−k+1:t)v_{t}=\mathrm{MLP}_{\mathrm{bias\text{-}free}}(\text{finite differences of }q_{t-k+1:t}) from a short window of pose codes. The predictor consumes only the current (qt,vt,at)(q_{t},v_{t},a_{t}), with no additional history, and outputs (q^t+1,v^t+1)(\hat{q}_{t+1},\hat{v}_{t+1}), both of which the loss supervises. Three design choices turned out to matter in practice, each discovered through a training failure rather than chosen a priori, and each analyzed in Section 8.

The motion head has to be bias-free. This is the mechanism that guarantees identical repeated frames give exactly zero finite difference and hence exactly zero decoded velocity, which makes vv a genuine motion code and not an arbitrary learned scalar. The predictor also has to be strictly memoryless: it sees only (qt,vt,at)(q_{t},v_{t},a_{t}) and no extra history window. Skipping this check is risky. An early version of our own pipeline compared TI-JEPA against a three-frame history baseline and produced a false negative, because the baseline’s history window quietly supplied the missing information; re-running against a matched-memory single-frame baseline caught the mistake. Finally, SIGReg has to be applied to qq alone, with a separate soft variance floor on vv. Applying it to the whole latent jointly collapses the representation to a degenerate fixed point, shown in Section 8.

The value of this split is not limited to raw rollout accuracy: because qq and vv are separate, named coordinates rather than entries in one undifferentiated vector, each can be probed and audited on its own, unlike an RSSM’s belief state, and this diagnosability is what lets Section 7.5 explain, not just report, where TI-JEPA and a recurrent aggregator agree and where they part ways.

6 RateIdent: Evaluation Protocols

Protocol A, probe ladder. With the encoder frozen and on held-out data, we fit four increasingly generous linear probes for ground-truth velocity: a single frame’s embedding, a pair of consecutive embeddings, the full kk-frame window, and, for TI-JEPA only, the explicit vtv_{t} channel. The train/test split is at the episode level rather than the frame level; an earlier, frame-level split produced a spurious R2≈0.86R^{2}\approx 0.86 purely from adjacent-frame leakage, which we caught and fixed.

Protocol B, kill experiment. We fix a configuration qq and construct two states differing only in velocity, vv and −v-v, and render both. By Proposition 1 the current frames are pixel-identical. We then compare each model’s blind, zero-action rollout against true forward simulation. A single environment-agnostic utility exploits time-reversal symmetry, negating velocity and stepping the real forward dynamics backward, to build valid contexts for physically different environments with no per-environment special-casing.

Protocol C, inertial planning. A stop-at-goal task using the cross-entropy method for planning (Rubinstein, 1997; Deng, 2006), whose cost, by Corollary 2, cannot be satisfied without implicitly using velocity. We run both an open-loop, single-shot variant and a closed-loop, receding-horizon variant in the style of model-predictive control (Williams et al., 2015; Nagabandi et al., 2018). Action budget and speed ratio are audited at environment design time, since an earlier, unaudited version let a velocity-blind planner brute-force the task with an oversized corrective action, masking the effect we wanted to measure.

7 Experiments

7.1 Official checkpoints, official benchmarks, no retraining

We run Protocol A directly on the four official real-world LeWM checkpoints, PushT, Reacher, Cube, and TwoRoom, using an episode-level split and RidgeCV, and compare each row to its own shuffled-label chance floor and to a ground-truth-position-only confound baseline.

Protocol B on the official PushT checkpoint, using the real pymunk simulator with damping overridden to 1.0 for this diagnostic only, gives a branch-separation ratio of 0.00870.0087 and a velocity-sign accuracy of 0.4750.475, at chance, despite ground-truth branches separating by more than 230 pixels over six seconds.

7.2 Matched-budget replication on real PushT pixels

Using the same cached PushT pixels and the same steps, batch size, and optimizer for both arms, TI-JEPA’s pose channel gives a 2.82.8 to 3.9×3.9\times larger held-out R2R^{2} than the baseline’s undifferentiated latent at the same window budget (window k=3k{=}3: 0.2940.294 versus 0.1010.101 for block velocity, 0.3960.396 versus 0.0380.038 for agent velocity), while both replicate the single-frame null exactly. Protocol B with the necessary matched-memory ablation gives the memoryless baseline a branch-separation ratio of exactly zero, sign accuracy exactly 0.5000.500, mathematically guaranteed by Corollary 1 rather than merely small; TI-JEPA, still memoryless, reaches sign accuracy 0.6500.650 and the lowest absolute rollout position error of all three real-PushT arms.

7.3 Three physically grounded environments

InertiaBall, Pendulum, and CartPole are built so that velocity is not optional: unactuated free motion, a gravity-restored pendulum, and a coupled cart-pole system, the latter two being the standard Gymnasium control tasks (Towers et al., 2024). All three share one CNN backbone and one hyperparameter recipe, with only physical constants and action budgets differing between environments.

Figure 4 gives the qualitative picture on Pendulum and CartPole: two context frames with identical configuration and opposite velocity are pixel-identical by construction, and in the blind rollout the memoryless baseline cannot separate the two velocity branches while TI-JEPA tracks the ground truth on both environments, at their two different coupling strengths. Table 3 reports Protocol C, stop-at-goal planning, against this matched-memory baseline (visualized across all three environments in Figure 11, Appendix E). Every closed-loop gap is statistically significant with p<10−9p<10^{-9} by a two-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test on matched tasks and seeds, and the InertiaBall result additionally replicates at an independent seed. On Pendulum, the memoryless baseline’s closed-loop corrections are actively harmful on average, worse than doing nothing.

7.4 Official-architecture scale validation

The largest open question after the results above is whether they survive a move from a small, from-scratch CNN to the actual official architecture family. We test this on both CartPole, the environment with the weakest small-CNN velocity probe, and Pendulum, the environment with the largest planning effect, so a scale effect cannot be attributed to a convenient single choice. The architecture is a from-scratch ViT-Tiny/14 encoder, hidden size 192, depth 12, three heads, with 224×224224\times 224 input, plus a six-layer, sixteen-head AdaLN-conditioned transformer predictor, matching the released official configuration. Getting this to train stably required matching the official optimizer exactly (AdamW, learning rate 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}, weight decay 10−310^{-3}, gradient clipping at 1.01.0, and a batch-norm projector head on both encoder and predictor outputs before the loss); a first attempt reusing the small-CNN recipe’s hyperparameters collapsed all three arms to a degenerate fixed point within a few hundred steps, reported as a methodology note in Appendix G. The corrected numbers below use the fixed recipe throughout.

Switching encoder family from a four-layer CNN to a global-attention ViT closes most of CartPole’s gap, raising the explicit velocity probe from r=0.30r{=}0.30 to r=0.91r{=}0.91 (Appendix E, Figure 12), while a within-family capacity ablation in Section 8 shows that simply adding parameters to the same CNN does not move this number at all. Together, these results trace the earlier CartPole ceiling to the small backbone’s limited spatial resolution. Across CartPole and Pendulum this is now five architecture/environment combinations in which the memoryless baseline’s branch separation is exactly zero and never merely small; a second training seed (Appendix D.5) reproduces this and moves the velocity probe by at most 0.0130.013.

7.5 Is TI-JEPA reinventing RSSM and Dreamer?

Recurrent belief-state world models solve a different-in-kind version of this problem by never committing to zt=E⁡(ot)z_{t}=E(o_{t}) as the read-out state (Section 2), so Proposition 1 does not apply to them. The method family we study moved away from recurrence instead, while its evaluated, probed, and planned-with representation stayed a single-frame embedding. To test this fairly, we replace the predictor’s window-concatenation aggregator with a GRU-cell recurrent aggregator over the same three-frame window, keeping the single-frame target and every probe or planner read-out identical.

Protocol A confirms the theory is untouched by this choice: the recurrent aggregator’s single-frame probe rr is −0.037-0.037, −0.008-0.008, and +0.037+0.037 on InertiaBall, Pendulum, and CartPole, statistically indistinguishable from chance in every case, exactly like every other single-frame-target encoder.

Table 5 splits by environment coupling strength. On InertiaBall and Pendulum, where the two coordinates evolve almost independently, the recurrent aggregator matches or slightly beats TI-JEPA’s branch-separation ratio and reaches the best closed-loop success rate of any learned model on both. On CartPole, the most nonlinearly coupled environment, the pattern reverses: branch separation 1.1521.152 for TI-JEPA against 0.6890.689 for the recurrent aggregator, and closed-loop success 0.2000.200 against 0.1200.120. The recurrent aggregator’s single opaque vector has to represent both rates without being told which part of it is which; TI-JEPA’s explicit split gives each rate its own coordinate, and that advantage shows up precisely where the coupling makes disentanglement hard. A second training seed (Appendix D) confirms this split; TI-JEPA stays the clear largest non-memoryless value on CartPole in both runs.

7.6 Real official-benchmark pixels at official scale: dm_control Reacher

This section combines every property tested separately so far, training from scratch at official ViT-Tiny plus AdaLN scale on real dm_control Reacher photographs, a torque-controlled, near-frictionless two-link arm and the one real benchmark among the four whose physics genuinely exercise this claim. Using the exact official-scale recipe from Section 7.4 with only the data source swapped, all three arms trained healthily with no collapse.

Pose decoding jumps from R2≈0.05R^{2}\approx 0.05–0.190.19 with the small CNN to R2≈0.68R^{2}\approx 0.68–0.940.94 with the official ViT, confirming the capacity-ceiling diagnosis for pose. The explicit velocity-to-true-angular-velocity probe, however, stays at exactly chance, and so does the memory-having baseline’s own richest, three-frame-window feature. The underlying dataset uses i.i.d. random torques, so true angular velocity decorrelates faster than our frame interval, limiting what any short-window estimator can recover regardless of architecture; Appendix F has the full analysis.

This is the largest TI-JEPA-versus-history-baseline branch-separation margin in the entire project, roughly 38×38\times, and the sixth independent combination, now on real photographic robot pixels, where the memoryless baseline’s branch separation is exactly zero at every horizon step, exactly as Corollary 1 guarantees. TI-JEPA’s branch-separation curve grows and eventually overtakes ground truth, on the same pixel-identical-start, opposite-velocity construction as the real-Reacher rows of Figure 3, while the history baseline’s stays essentially flat. Protocol A and B answer different questions here: vv is not a linear readout of true angular velocity (A), yet flipping vv’s sign changes the rollout more than for any baseline (B), so TI-JEPA’s motion channel learned sign-relevant structure even on a label that is itself only weakly resolved by any short window.

8 Ablations

Forcing v≡0v\equiv 0 by construction collapses the representation, and applying SIGReg to the whole latent z=(q,v)z=(q,v) jointly instead of to qq alone collapses it the same way, both reproduced bit-for-bit at an independent seed. A wider, deeper CNN backbone on CartPole (roughly 13×13\times more parameters) leaves the velocity probe flat (0.302→0.2980.302\to 0.298) and drops kill-experiment sign accuracy to chance (0.5250.525), so a backbone that trains stably can still lose the motion signal the small recipe recovers. Real PushT with default damping is scoped out of our planning claims (planner-side confound: Appendix G; full numbers: Appendix D).

9 Discussion and Limitations

CartPole’s velocity probe is modest (r≈0.30r\approx 0.30 at small-CNN scale) yet gives the largest closed-loop planning gain in the table: probe scores and downstream usability answer different questions, exactly Corollary 1’s mechanism. On limitations: Protocol B’s sign-accuracy metric sits at or below chance on both official-scale environments and on real Reacher, and real PushT downstream planning is a null result at our scale, so our positive planning claims stay scoped to three controlled synthetic environments. Full accounting: Appendices D and F.

10 Conclusion

We found a provable blind spot in the dominant next-frame JEPA recipe: a single-frame target cannot carry instantaneous velocity, for any encoder, because the renderer is instantaneous. Every result in this paper follows from that one argument. We confirmed it on official checkpoints with zero retraining, built environments where it cannot be avoided, fixed it with a lightweight pose/motion split that also improves planning, and reproduced the same guarantee at official model scale, against a recurrent-aggregator alternative, and on real robot pixels, where TI-JEPA shows its largest margin in the paper. The mechanism is simple, checkable, and now confirmed across six settings, with no privileged supervision and no extra history window at inference.

Appendix A Full formal theory

This appendix reproduces the complete formal statement summarized in Section 4, with full proofs, so that every claim in the main text is independently checkable.

A.1 Setup

Let (Ω,ℱ,ℙ)(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P}) be the underlying probability space and fix a possibly stochastic, possibly action-conditioned trajectory (qt,q˙t)t≥0(q_{t},\dot{q}_{t})_{t\geq 0} on 𝒬×ℝd\mathcal{Q}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}, with 𝒬⊆ℝd\mathcal{Q}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} open, together with actions (at)t≥0(a_{t})_{t\geq 0} on a measurable action space 𝒜\mathcal{A}. We make two assumptions, both satisfied by every next-frame JEPA world model we are aware of.

(P) Instantaneous rendering. There is a measurable rendering map g:𝒬→𝒪g:\mathcal{Q}\to\mathcal{O} such that the observation at time tt satisfies ot=g⁡(qt)o_{t}=g(q_{t}) almost surely. The pixel image depends on the trajectory only through the instantaneous configuration qtq_{t}, not through q˙t\dot{q}_{t}: no motion blur, no stroboscopic multi-exposure frames, no explicit velocity overlay.

(A) Single-frame encoder. The representation is produced by a deterministic, Borel-measurable map E:𝒪→𝒵E:\mathcal{O}\to\mathcal{Z} applied to one frame at a time, zt:=E⁡(ot)z_{t}:=E(o_{t}). EE may be an arbitrarily expressive neural network; measurability is the only requirement, so this covers every practically realizable encoder.

Write h:=E∘g:𝒬→𝒵h:=E\circ g:\mathcal{Q}\to\mathcal{Z}, itself Borel-measurable as a composition of Borel maps.

Definition (identifiability). A random variable vtv_{t} is identifiable from a random variable xtx_{t} if there exists a measurable function ϕ\phi with vt=ϕ⁡(xt)v_{t}=\phi(x_{t}) almost surely. Equivalently, vtv_{t} is σ⁡(xt)\sigma(x_{t})-measurable.

A.2 Proposition: single-frame targets cannot carry instantaneous rate

Proposition 1. Under (P) and (A), zt=h⁡(qt)z_{t}=h(q_{t}) almost surely, so ztz_{t} is σ⁡(qt)\sigma(q_{t})-measurable. Consequently, for any choice of EE: (1) data processing: every quantity identifiable from ztz_{t} is identifiable from qtq_{t}, σ⁡(zt)⊆σ⁡(qt)\sigma(z_{t})\subseteq\sigma(q_{t}); (2) non-identifiability of q˙\dot{q}: if q˙t\dot{q}_{t} is not almost surely a measurable function of qtq_{t} alone, equivalently the conditional law ℒ⁡(q˙t∣qt)\mathcal{L}(\dot{q}_{t}\mid q_{t}) is non-degenerate for a set of qtq_{t} of positive probability, then q˙t\dot{q}_{t} is not identifiable from ztz_{t}, for any encoder EE, however expressive; (3) conditional independence: zt⟂q˙t|qtz_{t}\perp\dot{q}_{t}\mid q_{t}.

Proof. (1) is immediate: zt=E⁡(g⁡(qt))=h⁡(qt)z_{t}=E(g(q_{t}))=h(q_{t}) is by construction a function of qtq_{t}, so any ϕ⁡(zt)=ϕ⁡(h⁡(qt))=:ψ⁡(qt)\phi(z_{t})=\phi(h(q_{t}))=:\psi(q_{t}) exhibiting identifiability from ztz_{t} also exhibits identifiability from qtq_{t} with ψ=ϕ∘h\psi=\phi\circ h. (2) is the contrapositive of (1) specialized to vt=q˙tv_{t}=\dot{q}_{t}: if q˙t\dot{q}_{t} were identifiable from zt=h⁡(qt)z_{t}=h(q_{t}) via some measurable ϕ\phi, then q˙t=ϕ⁡(h⁡(qt))\dot{q}_{t}=\phi(h(q_{t})) almost surely would exhibit q˙t\dot{q}_{t} as a measurable function of qtq_{t} alone, contradicting the hypothesis. (3) Since ztz_{t} is σ⁡(qt)\sigma(q_{t})-measurable, conditioning on qtq_{t} makes ztz_{t} degenerate, so for any bounded measurable f,ϕf,\phi, 𝔼⁡[f⁡(zt)​ϕ​(q˙t)∣qt]=f⁡(h⁡(qt))​𝔼​[ϕ⁡(q˙t)∣qt]=𝔼⁡[f⁡(zt)∣qt]​𝔼​[ϕ⁡(q˙t)∣qt]\mathbb{E}[f(z_{t})\phi(\dot{q}_{t})\mid q_{t}]=f(h(q_{t}))\,\mathbb{E}[\phi(\dot{q}_{t})\mid q_{t}]=\mathbb{E}[f(z_{t})\mid q_{t}]\,\mathbb{E}[\phi(\dot{q}_{t})\mid q_{t}]. ■\blacksquare

Remark, when the hypothesis of (2) fails. The only escape is the degenerate case where q˙t\dot{q}_{t} is itself a deterministic function of qtq_{t}, for example a first-order system disguised as second-order, or a trajectory confined to a single fixed-energy curve in phase space traversed in one direction only. This does not hold for any of our environments or for PushT, Reacher, Cube, or TwoRoom: in InertiaBall, Pendulum, and CartPole, the initial-condition distribution independently randomizes q0q_{0} and q˙0\dot{q}_{0}, so the same qq is visited with many different q˙\dot{q} across episodes, exactly what Protocol B’s opposite-velocity pairs exploit, and a pendulum in particular revisits the same angle each half-period with opposite-signed velocity within a single trajectory. The hypothesis of Proposition 1(2) is the generic, typically satisfied condition, not an idealized worst case.

A.3 Corollary: the JEPA predictor cannot use velocity, even though its numeric target does

Corollary 1. Let pred:𝒵×𝒜→𝒵\mathrm{pred}:\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{Z} range over all measurable functions and let pred⋆=arg⁡minpred​𝔼​‖pred⁡(zt,at)−zt+1‖2\mathrm{pred}^{\star}=\arg\min_{\mathrm{pred}}\mathbb{E}\|\mathrm{pred}(z_{t},a_{t})-z_{t+1}\|^{2} be the population-risk minimizer of the JEPA prediction loss. Then

pred⋆(z,a)=𝔼[zt+1∣zt=z,at=a]=𝔼[h(qt+1)∣h(qt)=z,at=a],\mathrm{pred}^{\star}(z,a)=\mathbb{E}[z_{t+1}\mid z_{t}=z,a_{t}=a]=\mathbb{E}[h(q_{t+1})\mid h(q_{t})=z,a_{t}=a],

that is, pred⋆\mathrm{pred}^{\star} is the q˙t\dot{q}_{t}-marginalized one-step transition. If the true transition kernel qt+1|(qt,q˙t,at)q_{t+1}\mid(q_{t},\dot{q}_{t},a_{t}) genuinely depends on q˙t\dot{q}_{t}, true for any non-degenerate second-order system, and the hypothesis of Proposition 1(2) holds, then pred⋆(zt,at)≠𝔼[zt+1∣qt,q˙t,at]\mathrm{pred}^{\star}(z_{t},a_{t})\neq\mathbb{E}[z_{t+1}\mid q_{t},\dot{q}_{t},a_{t}] with positive probability: the L2L^{2}-optimal single-frame-target predictor is provably not the correct one-step dynamics model.

Proof. The first equality is the standard fact that the conditional mean minimizes squared-error risk restricted to the σ⁡(zt,at)\sigma(z_{t},a_{t})-measurable function class. The second substitutes zt+1=h⁡(qt+1)z_{t+1}=h(q_{t+1}) and zt=h⁡(qt)z_{t}=h(q_{t}). For the final claim, by the tower property, 𝔼[h(qt+1)∣zt,at]=𝔼[𝔼[h(qt+1)∣qt,q˙t,at]∣zt,at]\mathbb{E}[h(q_{t+1})\mid z_{t},a_{t}]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[h(q_{t+1})\mid q_{t},\dot{q}_{t},a_{t}]\mid z_{t},a_{t}], so pred⋆\mathrm{pred}^{\star} is an average, over the conditional law of q˙t\dot{q}_{t} given (zt,at)(z_{t},a_{t}), of the true q˙t\dot{q}_{t}-dependent one-step map. When that map genuinely varies with q˙t\dot{q}_{t} and the averaging is over a non-degenerate law, the average differs from each individual branch on a positive-probability set, by Jensen’s inequality applied to the generically non-constant map q˙t↦𝔼[h(qt+1)∣qt,q˙t,at]\dot{q}_{t}\mapsto\mathbb{E}[h(q_{t+1})\mid q_{t},\dot{q}_{t},a_{t}]. ■\blacksquare

This is the formal statement behind the kill experiment. Two states with identical qtq_{t}, hence identical oto_{t}, hence identical ztz_{t}, but opposite q˙t=±v\dot{q}_{t}=\pm v, have by Corollary 1 the same pred⋆​(zt,at)\mathrm{pred}^{\star}(z_{t},a_{t}): the model’s best possible one-step prediction cannot distinguish them, and an open-loop rollout from them must coincide in the population limit, or, for a finite-capacity network approximating pred⋆\mathrm{pred}^{\star}, branch separation measured empirically should be near zero and decaying toward the population value as capacity and data grow. This matches the empirical finding on every environment we test: branch-sep(baselinek=1) is exactly zero, not merely small, on every one of the six environments in the paper.

A.4 Corollary: a single static goal image cannot specify a target velocity

Corollary 2. For any goal-conditioned planning objective of the form J(a0:H−1)=∥zH−E(og)∥22J(a_{0:H-1})=\|z_{H}-E(o_{g})\|_{2}^{2} with a single goal frame og=g⁡(qg)o_{g}=g(q_{g}), JJ depends on the planned trajectory’s terminal state only through h⁡(qH)h(q_{H}), hence JJ is constant on the fiber {(q,q˙):q=qH}\{(q,\dot{q}):q=q_{H}\} for any fixed qHq_{H}: such an objective cannot express a preference over terminal velocity and is minimized identically by any terminal velocity whatsoever.

Proof. Immediate from zH=h⁡(qH)z_{H}=h(q_{H}) depending on q˙H\dot{q}_{H} only vacuously. ■\blacksquare

This is the formal reason Protocol C’s stop-at-goal task is diagnostic: a planner whose cost is literally ‖zH−E⁡(og)‖2\|z_{H}-E(o_{g})\|^{2} has no way to prefer arriving slowly over arriving fast and coasting through, and must get whatever stopping behavior it exhibits from predictor accidents, not from the stated objective.

A.5 Three identifiability-restoring constructions

Each of the following replaces assumption (A) and is enough to break Proposition 1’s negative conclusion, that is, each makes q˙t\dot{q}_{t} identifiable in principle from the new target. We state the reason for each, then note what identifiability-in-principle does not imply, which is exactly what Protocol A’s probe ladder is measuring.

1. Multi-frame encoding, zt=E(ot−k:t)z_{t}=E(o_{t-k:t}) for k≥1k\geq 1. Now zt=h~(qt−k:t)z_{t}=\tilde{h}(q_{t-k:t}) for h~:=E∘(g,…,g)\tilde{h}:=E\circ(g,\dots,g), a function of k+1k+1 configurations, not one. If the dynamics are piecewise-differentiable and Δ​t\Delta t is the frame interval, q˙t=(qt−qt−1)/Δ​t+O⁡(Δ​t)\dot{q}_{t}=(q_{t}-q_{t-1})/\Delta t+O(\Delta t) is a measurable, in fact continuous, function of the window, so the necessary condition of Proposition 1(1) no longer forecloses identifiability. This is exactly the official predictor’s three-frame history input, but history reaching the predictor does not put velocity in zz itself, since the target is still a single frame’s embedding, which is precisely the distinction Protocol B’s baselinek=1 versus baselinek=3 arms are built to separate.

2. Structured target, zt=(qt,vt)z_{t}=(q_{t},v_{t}) with qt=Eq​(ot)q_{t}=E_{q}(o_{t}) single-frame and vt=Ev(ot−k+1:t)v_{t}=E_{v}(o_{t-k+1:t}) an explicit function of a finite-difference window, and, critically, the JEPA prediction target becomes zt+1=(qt+1,vt+1)z_{t+1}=(q_{t+1},v_{t+1}) rather than zt+1=E⁡(ot+1)z_{t+1}=E(o_{t+1}) alone, that is, the velocity head’s own output enters what is being predicted, not only what is being predicted from. This is TI-JEPA. Formally it is a special case of construction 1 that additionally forces the q˙\dot{q}-carrying part of zz to be exposed as its own coordinate rather than left implicit inside an opaque multi-frame function, which is what makes it linearly probeable by design rather than merely information-theoretically present.

3. Predict the transition itself: supervise Δ​zt:=zt+1−zt\Delta z_{t}:=z_{t+1}-z_{t} rather than zt+1z_{t+1} directly. Since Δ​qt≈q˙t​Δ​t\Delta q_{t}\approx\dot{q}_{t}\,\Delta t, a target built from consecutive frame differences is, by the same argument as construction 1, a function of a two-frame window and hence not subject to Proposition 1’s single-frame hypothesis.

This project implements the lightweight combination of constructions 1 and 2: frame stacking into the encoder together with an explicit, structurally separated pose and motion split in zz.

Remark, identifiability-in-principle versus linear decodability. Constructions 1 through 3 each restore identifiability in the definitional sense, some measurable ϕ\phi exists, but say nothing about whether a specific finite encoder, trained with a specific loss and optimizer on finite data, represents q˙t\dot{q}_{t} in an easily decodable, for example linear, way. This is exactly the gap Protocol A is designed to expose, and it is why CartPole’s small-CNN vtv_{t} Pearson r≈0.30r\approx 0.30, present, well above the single-frame floor of approximately zero, but weaker than InertiaBall’s 0.570.57 or Pendulum’s 0.880.88, is not a theoretical anomaly. The theorem only guarantees q˙t\dot{q}_{t} is no longer measure-theoretically excluded once assumption (A) is dropped; whether a small bias-free MLP acting on a four-layer CNN’s features finds an easily linear encoding of two coupled physical degrees of freedom from low-resolution pixels is an orthogonal, empirical, capacity and optimization question, which Section 7.4’s encoder-family ablation and Appendix D’s within-family capacity ablation together narrow down to backbone spatial resolution rather than embedding dimensionality.

A.6 What this theory does not claim

It does not claim single-frame JEPA representations are useless for physical understanding, only that a specific, narrow, well-defined quantity, instantaneous rate of change of configuration, is excluded from a specific, narrow, well-defined target construction. Configuration variables, position, angle, joint pose, are not covered by Proposition 1 and are exactly what LeWM’s own probing tables measure well. It does not claim pair-based fixes such as PSG-JEPA or Delta-JEPA are wrong; construction 1 above is a formalization of what they do, and Proposition 1 is precisely why grounding a pair is a valid fix. The distinction we draw is that a pair-decodable quantity need not be single-frame-decodable, which is the distinction Protocol A’s single, pair, window, and explicit-vv ladder is built to expose as four different, ordered empirical claims rather than one. It does not require any particular parametric family for EE: the proof only uses Borel measurability, so it applies unchanged to a ViT-Tiny ImageNet-scale encoder exactly as much as to a small CNN, which is the formal reason the official-checkpoint result on real PushT, branch-sep near zero, sign accuracy near chance, measured on the actual released weights, is not a toy-model artifact.

Appendix B Extended related-work discussion: the RSSM and Dreamer boundary

This appendix expands the argument summarized in Section 2 and tested in Section 7.5, since it is the single most obvious objection a knowledgeable reviewer will raise: why is this not simply reinventing PlaNet.

Recurrent state-space world models solved a version of our problem years earlier by refusing to commit to zt=E⁡(ot)z_{t}=E(o_{t}) as the object anything downstream reads. PlaNet’s actual state is the pair (ht,st)(h_{t},s_{t}), where the deterministic path hth_{t} is fed by the previous state and action and can therefore integrate information across unboundedly many past frames. This is simply a different mathematical object than a single-frame embedding, and Proposition 1’s hypothesis (A) does not describe it. If a world model’s read-out state is hth_{t}-like, our theorem is vacuous for it, and we do not claim otherwise.

The reason this observation does not make our contribution redundant is that the specific family of methods we study, LeWM and its 2026 JEPA follow-ups, made a different design choice than PlaNet and Dreamer, for reasons orthogonal to velocity: they moved away from recurrent belief states specifically to get training stability, parallelism, and compatibility with modern non-generative self-supervised regularizers that motivate the whole JEPA line, and their actual evaluated, probed, and planned-with representation is the single-frame zt=E⁡(ot)z_{t}=E(o_{t}). The predictor’s optional history window is a training-time convenience, not the object anything downstream reads, which is exactly the distinction construction 1 in Appendix A flags: multi-frame encoding of the input is not the same as putting velocity into the target. Given that this design choice is already fixed across the whole method family, reverting to a full recurrent belief state is a valid fix in principle but a different, heavier paper than the one we are writing; it would mean reworking what the representation is for the entire evaluated family, not patching it.

What we can and do test, as the fair, minimal, same-footprint version of the recurrence question that stays inside the single-frame-zz-as-state paradigm every method in our comparison table actually uses, is replacing the history-window aggregator with a GRU-cell recurrent aggregator that consumes the same kk-frame window through a recurrent hidden state instead of flattening it, while keeping the single-frame zt=E⁡(ot)z_{t}=E(o_{t}) as the only thing anything downstream, probes, kill-experiment rollout, planning cost, ever reads. This deliberately does not attempt to reproduce full PlaNet or Dreamer, which would also require changing the probing and planning protocol to read out hth_{t}, a different and larger experiment than an ablation of one paper’s aggregator choice. It answers the narrower, fair question of whether recurrence-as-aggregator alone, the part of RSSM’s design that is cheap to bolt onto an existing pipeline, is sufficient, or whether the target-construction problem Proposition 1 identifies survives it. Section 7.5 reports the result, and we explicitly did not cherry-pick which environments to show.

Explicitly out of scope as a main contribution framing, stated up front so it cannot be read as scope creep later: reporting one more joint-velocity probe number in isolation; adding a proprioception-grounding head; showing Δ​z→a\Delta z\to a is invertible; success rate on PushT or OGBench goal-image tasks as the headline metric; violation-of-expectation physics benchmarks as a main table; simply concatenating PSG’s and Delta’s constructions; or reproducing a full PlaNet or Dreamer-style recurrent belief state and claiming that as our fix. Each of these is either already someone else’s contribution or does not by itself distinguish our claim from theirs.

Appendix C Full experimental setup and hyperparameters

C.1 Small-CNN recipe (InertiaBall, Pendulum, CartPole, and the RSSM ablation)

All three custom environments and the recurrent-aggregator ablation share one architecture family and one hyperparameter recipe by design, to rule out per-environment tuning as a confound. Encoder: a four-layer convolutional backbone (ConvBackbone), channel widths (32,64,64,64)(32,64,64,64), feeding a linear head to z​_​d​i​m=8z\_dim=8 for the baseline family or q​_​d​i​m=v​_​d​i​m=4q\_dim=v\_dim=4 for TI-JEPA. Predictor: a small MLP-based history predictor consuming a k=3k=3 window (baselinek=3), a memoryless variant consuming k=1k=1 (baselinek=1), a GRU-cell recurrent aggregator consuming the same k=3k=3 window through a hidden state (baselinernn), or TI-JEPA’s memoryless (qt,vt,at)→(q^t+1,v^t+1)(q_{t},v_{t},a_{t})\to(\hat{q}_{t+1},\hat{v}_{t+1}) predictor. Optimizer: Adam, learning rate 10−310^{-3}, batch size 256256, 80008000 training steps, λreg=1.0\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}}=1.0 (SIGReg weight on qq, or on zz for the baseline family), λv=0.1\lambda_{v}=0.1 (variance floor weight on vv, TI-JEPA only). Images are rendered at 64×6464\times 64 resolution. No gradient clipping, no projector head. This is deliberately the simplest recipe that trains stably, so that any effect found is not attributable to an elaborate training procedure.

C.2 Official ViT-Tiny plus AdaLN-transformer recipe (official-scale CartPole, Pendulum, and real Reacher)

Encoder: a from-scratch ViT-Tiny/14 patch embedding, hidden size 192192, depth 1212, three attention heads, 224×224224\times 224 input resolution, matching the released official configuration exactly (not routed through any external backbone library, to avoid an unnecessary heavy dependency while remaining architecturally identical). Predictor: a six-layer, sixteen-head AdaLN-zero-conditioned transformer, mlp_dim=2048=2048, consuming a three-frame window for the baseline family or the current (qt,vt,at)(q_{t},v_{t},a_{t}) for TI-JEPA. Total parameter count is approximately 16.516.5M, versus under 11M for the small-CNN recipe. Optimizer: AdamW, learning rate 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}, weight decay 10−310^{-3}, gradient-norm clipping at 1.01.0, batch size matched to the small-CNN recipe. A batch-norm-containing MLP projector head is applied to both the encoder’s and the predictor’s outputs before the loss, a standard anti-collapse mechanism in this style of self-supervised method. λreg=5.0\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}}=5.0 and λv=1.0\lambda_{v}=1.0, both raised from the small-CNN recipe’s defaults after a short diagnostic sweep described in Appendix G. Training runs 50005000 steps per arm. All three arms per environment, baselinek=3, baselinek=1, and TI-JEPA, were run strictly sequentially rather than concurrently, since each process’s real GPU and CPU memory footprint at this scale was too large for safe concurrent execution on a single 46GB GPU and 50GB host memory budget.

For real Reacher, the training pixels come from a cached, native 224×224224\times 224 resolution window dataset built from dm_control’s Reacher random-policy rollouts, 600 episodes, 40,200 decimated frames after a frameskip of 3 raw environment steps (12,200ms wall time per model step). Every other hyperparameter is identical to the official-scale synthetic recipe.

Appendix D Full result tables and ablations

D.1 Negative controls

D.2 Cross-scale summary

Including InertiaBall’s small-CNN result and real Reacher’s official-scale result, the memoryless baseline’s branch separation is exactly zero in six independent architecture, environment, and dataset combinations: three small-CNN synthetic environments, two official-scale synthetic environments, and one official-scale real-benchmark environment. This is the single most repeated piece of evidence for the paper’s core theoretical claim, and it never once comes out small but nonzero, exactly what Proposition 1 and Corollary 1 predict for a proof that depends only on Borel measurability rather than on any property of a specific encoder family.

D.3 Recurrent-aggregator ablation, full protocol A numbers

The recurrent aggregator’s pair and window rungs show the predictor can extract motion information implicitly from multi-frame input, the same phenomenon baselinek=3 already exhibits, but there is no single, separately regularized, linearly decodable code to point to the way TI-JEPA’s explicit vtv_{t} probe provides. This is the concrete sense in which Protocol A’s core claim, no single-frame-target encoder has a linearly decodable velocity code in ztz_{t} itself, is invariant to the choice of aggregation mechanism.

Note on evaluation-code versioning. The recurrent-aggregator ablation required re-running the kill experiment and planning scripts from scratch, to get all four arms, including the new recurrent arm, evaluated on identically sampled pairs and tasks in one execution. This re-run’s CartPole and Pendulum branch-separation numbers for baselinek=3 and TI-JEPA differ slightly from an earlier, solo three-arm run of the same checkpoints under an older version of the environment and evaluation code, touched multiple times during the project’s long session, most recently for the official-scale debugging described in Appendix G. We adopted the re-run’s numbers as canonical throughout this paper, since they are the ones actually exercised by every table that involves the recurrent-aggregator comparison, and we confirmed them twice, immediately below, giving CartPole 0.2080.208/1.1521.152 and Pendulum 1.1171.117/1.0711.071 for baselinek=3/TI-JEPA exactly both times. InertiaBall was unaffected. The qualitative pattern that matters for the paper’s claims, baselinek=1’s branch separation exactly zero and TI-JEPA the largest non-baselinek=1 value on CartPole, holds under both the old and new numbers.

D.4 Recurrent-aggregator ablation, second independent training seed

The comparison in Section 7.5 trains one recurrent-aggregator arm per environment. To check how much of the picture depends on that single training run, we trained a second baseline_rnn arm per environment from a different random seed (weight initialization and minibatch order; the held-out evaluation data and the baselinek=1/baselinek=3/TI-JEPA checkpoints are unchanged, so the two seeds are directly comparable) and re-ran Protocols A, B, and C against the same fixed checkpoints.

Two things hold up across the second seed. First, on InertiaBall and Pendulum the recurrent aggregator’s branch-separation ratio and closed-loop success stay at or above TI-JEPA’s in both seeds, confirming the tie is not a one-seed artifact. Second, and more interesting, on CartPole the recurrent aggregator’s own result turns out to be the less stable one: branch separation swings from 0.6890.689 down to 0.0910.091, a value close to the memoryless baselinek=1’s exact zero, while the closed-loop success rate drops from 0.1200.120 to 0.0900.090, now below baselinek=3’s 0.1100.110. TI-JEPA’s CartPole numbers, by contrast, are the same fixed checkpoint evaluated both times and are the clear largest value in the table in both runs. This does not let us claim TI-JEPA itself is more seed-robust, since only the recurrent arm was retrained with a second seed here, but it does resolve the most likely follow-up question about Section 7.5: the CartPole advantage for TI-JEPA over the recurrent aggregator is not an artifact of a single lucky training run of the competing baseline, it holds, and by a larger margin, in both of the two seeds we have tried.

Success rate is a thresholded metric, so we also report the underlying mean final distance to goal for the same closed-loop MPC runs, oracle included, in Table 11.

The raw distance numbers tell the same story as the success-rate table on the environment that matters most for our claims: on CartPole, TI-JEPA’s mean final distance (0.1750.175) is the lowest of the three learned arms in both seeds, while the recurrent aggregator (0.2370.237/0.2350.235) stays close to the memory-matched baseline (0.2400.240) and does not close the gap. On InertiaBall the recurrent aggregator is the best learned arm by this metric too, in both seeds, consistent with the tie reported above. Pendulum shows the one place where the two metrics disagree: the recurrent aggregator’s seed-0 mean distance (0.1340.134) is the best of the three, but its seed-2 mean distance (0.1880.188) is the worst, even though its seed-2 success rate (0.3700.370) still exceeds TI-JEPA’s (0.2700.270); thresholded success rate and raw distance can rank runs differently near the success boundary, which is why we report both.

D.5 Official-scale results, second independent training seed

Section 7.4’s official ViT-Tiny plus AdaLN-transformer results for CartPole and Pendulum are each from one training run per arm. We retrained all three arms (baselinek=1, baselinek=3, TI-JEPA) for both environments from an independent seed (seed 22 instead of seed 00), using the identical recipe, and re-ran Protocols A and B. Table 12 reports both seeds side by side.

The headline number is the most stable one: the explicit velocity probe rr moves by at most 0.0130.013 across seeds on either environment, so the capacity-ceiling fix from switching encoder families is not a one-run fluke. baselinek=1’s branch separation is exactly zero in both seeds on both environments, again exactly as Proposition 1 and Corollary 1 require regardless of training seed. The remaining numbers move more: on CartPole, TI-JEPA stays the clear largest non-baselinek=1 branch-separation value and the lowest rollout MSE in both seeds, so its qualitative advantage there is seed-robust, though the absolute margins are larger in seed 2. On Pendulum, baselinek=3 already exceeded TI-JEPA’s branch-separation ratio in the original seed, an effect we attribute to a coasting-trajectory overshoot rather than better velocity use, and the same pattern holds, more strongly, in seed 2 (3.6083.608 versus 1.8951.895); baselinek=3’s rollout MSE also flips from best in seed 0 (0.3910.391) to worst in seed 2 (1.2611.261), the largest seed-to-seed swing in this table. We read this as Pendulum’s dynamics being more sensitive to training noise for the raw-rollout metrics specifically, not as evidence against the identifiability claim itself, which is exactly the claim that does not move.

This section collects every qualitative figure produced for this project, redrawn with a single consistent color code (ground truth black, baselinek=1 red, baselinek=3 orange, the recurrent-aggregator baseline purple, TI-JEPA blue) so the whole appendix reads as one coherent picture rather than a collection of separately generated debug plots. Each kill-experiment figure below pairs a real, high-resolution frame strip of the actual open-loop rollout, showing the two opposite-velocity branches starting pixel-identical and physically diverging, with the corresponding decoded blind-rollout curve for every arm trained on that environment.

E.1 Frame-by-frame visualization of branch divergence, many independent examples

The figures above each show one representative pair per environment. To demonstrate that the divergence is a generic property of the construction rather than a cherry-picked example, this subsection gives four independent, randomly drawn same-q0q_{0}-opposite-velocity pairs per environment, each rendered as an eight-frame strip for both branches (so every panel below is an 8×88\times 8 grid of real rendered frames, sixty-four images per environment, two hundred and fifty-six in total across the four environments). Appendix F Full accounting of limitations

We list here, without softening, every limitation identified over the course of this project, most of which are summarized more briefly in Section 9.

  1. 1.

    Official full-architecture-scale reproduction is done for CartPole and Pendulum, now at two independent training seeds each (Appendix D.5). The theory-mandated claim, baselinek=1’s branch separation exactly zero, reproduces exactly in all four runs. TI-JEPA’s explicit velocity probe on CartPole improves dramatically over the small-CNN recipe, 0.30→0.910.30\to 0.91, stable across both seeds (0.9100.910/0.9110.911); Pendulum’s stays roughly flat and already strong, 0.879→0.8320.879\to 0.832/0.8190.819. One genuine open wrinkle: Protocol B’s sign-accuracy metric is noisy at n=150n=150 pairs, at or below chance on CartPole in both seeds (0.2130.213, 0.2270.227) but landing on opposite sides of chance on Pendulum across the two seeds (0.4470.447, 0.6200.620), consistent with sampling noise on a binary metric at this nn rather than a systematic bias, though the underlying sign convention issue raised below is not yet fully resolved either way.

  2. 2.

    CartPole’s small-CNN explicit velocity probe was the weakest of the three synthetic environments, r≈0.30r\approx 0.30, and did not improve along either of two capacity axes tested within the CNN family. A wider CNN specifically degraded the kill-experiment sign accuracy to chance. Section 7.4 shows this ceiling is specific to the small-CNN family, not to CartPole or to TI-JEPA: switching encoder family raises the same probe to r=0.91r=0.91. The within-family capacity results should be read as a statement about this specific small CNN’s spatial resolution and inductive bias, not about CartPole’s velocity being fundamentally hard to expose.

  3. 3.

    CartPole’s open-loop planning gap, 31%, is more modest than its closed-loop gap, 64%; both arms are far from oracle under a strict success threshold, so closed-loop MPC is the more reliable readout for this environment.

  4. 4.

    Real PushT downstream planning is a null result: no evidence for or against the planning claim at this scale and compute budget on real contact dynamics; the positive planning results are scoped to the three controlled synthetic environments.

  5. 5.

    All three synthetic environments share one model family and training recipe by design, to rule out per-environment tuning as a confound. Section 7.4 is the first test of a genuinely different encoder and predictor family.

  6. 6.

    Protocol C’s statistical tests, paired Wilcoxon, n=100n=100 to 200200 tasks, draw tasks from one fixed distribution per environment, one speed range, one goal-radius interval; generalization to a broader or more extreme task distribution is untested.

  7. 7.

    The cross-entropy method is not a state-of-the-art planner; whether the observed gap persists, shrinks, or grows under a stronger planner such as MPPI or a learned policy is untested.

  8. 8.

    Section 7.5’s recurrent-aggregator ablation is a mixed result rather than a clean win: on InertiaBall and Pendulum, the recurrent aggregator ties or beats TI-JEPA on raw rollout and planning metrics, though never on Protocol A’s core identifiability claim, which is unaffected by aggregator choice on all three environments. TI-JEPA’s advantage on raw task performance is clearly demonstrated only on CartPole, and we offer a plausible explanation, structural disentanglement matters most when multiple physically distinct rates must be told apart, but do not have a fourth environment to confirm it generalizes.

  9. 9.

    Section 7.6’s real-Reacher official-scale result has an internal split between the two protocols: Protocol B shows TI-JEPA’s largest margin in the paper, but Protocol A shows the explicit velocity code is not a linear readout of true angular velocity on this specific real dataset, traced to the training distribution’s fast-decorrelating, independently and identically distributed random-torque action statistics rather than to architecture, since even the memory-having baseline’s richest feature fails the same linear probe, but not independently confirmed on a second real benchmark with different action statistics.

  10. 10.

    We ran one direct check of the decorrelation explanation above: rebuilding the real-Reacher cache with frameskip 11 instead of 33, the shortest possible frame interval, on the same official-scale recipe (220 episodes, matched to the original cache’s total frame count, since raw frameskip-1 storage at the original 4000-episode setting would not fit in memory). If decorrelation were the whole story, a shorter interval should recover some qvel signal. It did not: the explicit vtv_{t} probe’s qvel R2R^{2} stayed at −0.03-0.03 to −0.04-0.04, still chance, for every arm. It also did not cleanly refute the explanation, because pose decoding itself degraded at this frameskip, baselinek=3’s pose4 R2R^{2} fell to −0.05-0.05 and TI-JEPA’s to −0.01-0.01, compared to 0.680.68–0.940.94 at frameskip 33, most likely because the true per-frame displacement at frameskip 11 is smaller than the encoder’s own pixel-level noise floor, confounded further by the smaller episode count this cache needed to stay within memory. This test is inconclusive rather than confirmatory, and we report it as an honest attempt that did not resolve the question, not as supporting evidence either way.

Appendix G Methodology notes and self-caught issues

We report the following methodology issues in detail because each is a real trap that we fell into and corrected during the project, and each is a trap available to any future work attempting a similar comparison, not only to us.

Frame-level versus episode-level probe splits. An early version of Protocol A split train and test data at the frame level rather than the episode level. This produced a spurious R2≈0.86R^{2}\approx 0.86 for velocity purely from adjacent-frame leakage between train and test, since consecutive frames within an episode are highly correlated. Fixed by switching to an episode-level split and reported here as a methodology note, since this is a realistic trap for anyone building a similar probe on sequential data.

Confounding memory with structure in Protocol C. An early version of our Protocol C pipeline compared TI-JEPA’s memoryless predictor against a k=3k=3 history-window baseline and produced a false negative: TI-JEPA looked worse. This was caught only by re-running against a matched-memory baselinek=1 ablation, which showed the earlier comparison had confounded whether the structured latent z=(q,v)z=(q,v) itself was sufficient with whether the baseline’s history window was quietly supplying the missing velocity information.

Action-budget audit. An earlier, unaudited version of the Pendulum and CartPole environments let a completely velocity-blind planner brute-force the stop-at-goal task with a large enough single corrective action, masking the effect we wanted to measure. We built an explicit action-budget and speed-ratio audit at environment-design time to rule this out before running the reported Protocol C numbers.

Official-scale hyperparameter collapse. A first attempt at the official ViT-Tiny plus AdaLN-transformer scale-validation run reused the small-CNN recipe’s hyperparameters verbatim, learning rate 10−310^{-3}, plain Adam, λreg=1.0\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}}=1.0, no gradient clipping, no projector head. All three arms, including both baselines, collapsed to a degenerate fixed point, zstd/vstd→0z_{\mathrm{std}}/v_{\mathrm{std}}\to 0 monotonically, the SIGReg loss freezing at the same fingerprint value seen in the forced-collapse ablations in Appendix D, within a few hundred steps. This is a hyperparameter and optimization artifact, not a finding about identifiability at scale. The released official configuration uses learning rate 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}, AdamW with weight decay 10−310^{-3}, gradient-norm clipping at 1.01.0, and a batch-norm-containing MLP projector applied to both the encoder’s and the predictor’s outputs before the loss, a standard anti-collapse mechanism in this style of self-supervised method. We ported the projector, switched to AdamW with gradient clipping, and used the official learning rate. Because our from-scratch SIGReg implementation’s normalization differs from the official one, we could not assume the official λreg=0.09\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}}=0.09 transferred unchanged, and instead re-swept it on short, 600-step diagnostic runs: λreg∈{0.09,1.0}\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}}\in\{0.09,1.0\} still collapsed, while λreg=5.0\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}}=5.0 kept zstdz_{\mathrm{std}} stable and non-degenerate, moving from 0.300.30 to 0.850.85 rather than monotonically to zero; λv\lambda_{v} was similarly raised from 0.10.1 to 1.01.0. All official-scale numbers reported in the paper use this corrected recipe; the invalid first-pass numbers were discarded rather than reported.

Cache-build memory limits. Building the real Reacher dataset cache initially targeted 4000 episodes, which we estimated would produce a roughly 40GB cache. This process died silently under nohup with no error trace. We diagnosed this as an out-of-memory kill under a tighter-than-expected cgroup memory limit, roughly 50GB total against roughly 32GB already used by other processes on the shared host, rather than a code bug. We reduced the target to 600 episodes, producing a 6.05GB cache, and reran the build in the foreground to confirm no further errors, after which the reduced cache trained all three official-scale Reacher arms without incident.

HDF5 read performance. A first version of the cache-build script read decimated frames directly with strided fancy indexing from the source HDF5 file, which measured at roughly 1.8 seconds per 201-frame episode. We found that h5py’s strided reads on this dataset were roughly 10×10\times slower than a single contiguous read of the same span, 1.6 versus 0.15 to 0.27 seconds per episode, and switched to reading the full contiguous block once per episode and decimating with plain NumPy slicing afterward, reducing per-episode processing time to roughly 0.05 seconds.
